title: Conditional Rendering
subtitle: &&, ternary, early return, and null — showing UI based on state
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: UIs have many states — loading, empty, error, authenticated/unauthenticated. Rendering different UI for different states requires conditional logic.
whyItExists.solution: React's JSX is JavaScript, so you can use all of JavaScript's conditional tools. The key insight: JSX can only hold expressions (not statements like if/else), but expressions are enough — ternary, &&, and early return cover every case.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any time the UI should look different based on state: loading spinners, error messages, empty states, authenticated content, feature flags.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Avoid deeply nested ternaries (A ? B ? C : D : E) — they're hard to read. Extract into a variable or a separate function. If you have more than two states, use an object/map pattern or a switch statement before the JSX.

explainModes.beginner: To show something only when a condition is true, use && in JSX: {isLoggedIn && <UserMenu />}. To show one of two things, use a ternary: {isLoggedIn ? <LogoutButton /> : <LoginButton />}. To show nothing at all, return null from a component.
explainModes.simple:
Three patterns: (1) && — show only if true: {count > 0 &&

Items: {count}

}. (2) ternary — show one of two: {isLoading ? : }. (3) early return — return null or a fallback early in the function. Gotcha: {0 && } renders 0, not nothing — use {count > 0 && }. false, null, undefined render nothing; 0 and '' render.
explainModes.standard:
Storing JSX in a variable: const content = condition ? : ; return
{content}
. Extracting render functions: const renderStatus = () => { if (loading) return ; if (error) return ; return ; }. Null component pattern: function Guard({ canView, children }) { if (!canView) return null; return children; }.
explainModes.technical: React's reconciler treats null, undefined, false, and true as 'render nothing' — they produce no DOM nodes. This is by design, enabling the && pattern. Note: 0 is a falsy JS value but React renders it as the text '0' — it's not null/undefined/boolean, it's a number. Type-safe conditional: TypeScript + discriminated unions let the compiler ensure you handle every state. Loading/error/success is a classic union type.
explainModes.deepDive: Suspense: a modern alternative to manual loading states. Wrap components that may suspend with <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>. The child component (or data library) calls a special 'suspend' mechanism when data isn't ready — React shows the fallback. This composes: nested Suspense boundaries show the nearest fallback. React 18 Suspense supports server-side rendering and streaming. Error boundaries (class components that implement componentDidCatch) catch rendering errors in their subtree — they're the 'catch' of conditional rendering for exceptions.

questions.question: Which values render nothing in React JSX?
options: false, null, undefined, 0, and empty string ''
questions.explanation: false, null, undefined, and true all render nothing in JSX. 0 and '' (empty string) DO render — 0 shows as the text '0', and '' shows nothing visually but is still a valid string. This is why {count && <X />} is dangerous when count can be 0: it renders '0' instead of nothing. Use {count > 0 && <X />} to be safe.

faq.q: When should I use ternary vs &&?
faq.a: Use && when you want to show something only if true, and show nothing otherwise. Use ternary when you have two alternatives (show A or show B). For more than two states, extract a variable or a function before the return statement rather than nesting ternaries.
